title: Inside Parliament
rule: Every fact on the Inside Parliament screen names a source in this file. V means checked on the official page itself; S means taken from a reputable secondary source and labelled as such. Roles are described, not named: who holds each role changes, so every role links to the official page that says who holds it now. Nothing here comes from private or internal briefings.
lede: How Parliament actually runs: its year, its week and its day, what a Member of Youth Parliament, an MP and a peer each do with their time, who keeps the place working, the building itself, and who changes the rules. Written for young people; it points to UK Youth Parliament and UK Parliament pages rather than repeating them.

year.d: Marks the formal start of the parliamentary year. The King gives a speech from the throne in the House of Lords; the Government writes it, and it sets out the laws it plans for the new session.

year.t: One meeting of all three parts
year.d: State Opening is the only regular time the Sovereign, the House of Lords and the House of Commons all meet together. The Commons doors are shut in Black Rod's face, a sign of the Commons' independence that dates back to the Civil War.
A new session begins with State Opening, held on the first day of a new session or shortly after a general election.
Breaks when neither House sits, formally called periodic adjournments. The calendar of sitting days is announced by the Leader of the House of Commons as far ahead as practicable.

year.t: Why it matters for a campaign
year.d: Neither House sits in recess, so nothing is debated then. Time launches and asks for sitting weeks.

week.hours: Afternoons; the start time has changed by resolution of the House, so check the Order Paper
E-petitions can be recommended by the Petitions Committee for debate here

week_note: Finishing times are approximate and none of these apply in recess. The House of Lords consulted in 2026 on starting earlier on Tuesdays and Wednesdays; its committee expects to report in January 2027, so these times may change.

day.d: Every Commons sitting opens with prayers.
MPs question the ministers of one department; the Order Paper names which. Prime Minister's Questions starts at noon on Wednesdays.
Business that can happen at short notice, so it is not always on the Order Paper.
The Leader of the House announces next week's business and, usually, provisional business for the week after. MPs then question the Leader on it, often asking for debates or statements.
Debates on Bills and motions. Which Bill, and which stage, is set out on that day's Order Paper.
A half-hour debate where one backbench MP raises an issue and the relevant minister replies.

orderpaper.d: A summary of the day's business in the Chamber and in Westminster Hall.
The Chamber's business in order, then Westminster Hall, written statements, committees meeting today and committee reports published.
Deadlines for asking for debates, business chosen by the Backbench Business Committee and, near recesses, dates for tabling questions.
The calendar of business already timetabled for later days.
Urgent questions, oral statements and emergency debates can happen at short notice and do not appear in advance.

life_intro: Three ways of representing people, side by side. The UK Youth Parliament's own guides explain the MYP role in full; this comparison is here so you can see how it sits next to the adult roles.

life.who: A young person aged 11 to 18, elected by young people in their area.
life.time: On average 1 to 5 hours a week on UK Youth Parliament activities. A term usually lasts two years.
life.where: Their local area, regional meetings, and the UK Youth Parliament's annual sitting, which can be held at Westminster.
rhythm: Represents young people in their area
Works with their local team and other MYPs
Takes part in consultations and shares young people's views
Helps run Make Your Mark, the UK's largest youth ballot

life.who: One of 650 MPs, each elected by the voters of one constituency.
life.time: Divided between Westminster and the constituency. Professor Emma Crewe's research follows one MP through a Tuesday at Westminster and another through a Friday in a constituency four hours' travel away.
life.where: The Chamber, Westminster Hall, committee rooms, their office, and the constituency.
rhythm: Westminster: the Chamber, Westminster Hall, committees, votes and meetings
Evenings: research and speech writing for the next day's debate
Constituency: local visits, casework and time with family who live there
life.own: A real Tuesday in Westminster and a Friday in the constituency, from Professor Emma Crewe's research

life.role: Peer (member of the House of Lords)
life.who: Appointed, not elected. Most sit for a party; Crossbench peers sit as independents, some recommended by the House of Lords Appointments Commission from public applications.
life.time: The House sits from 2.30pm on Monday and Tuesday, 3pm on Wednesday and 11am on Thursday. Crossbench peers often fit the House around careers outside.
life.where: The Lords Chamber, Grand Committee and Lords committees.
rhythm: Oral questions to the Government at the start of the sitting, for about 30 minutes
Line-by-line checking of Bills, at committee and report stages
life.own: UK Parliament's own guide to the House of Lords' sitting times and questions

roles.role: Speaker of the House of Commons
roles.d: Chairs debates in the Commons as a neutral referee, making sure the rules are followed and order kept. The Speaker must be politically impartial.
roles.youth: The Speaker decides which MPs get to speak and which urgent questions are granted.

roles.role: Leader of the House of Commons
roles.d: A Cabinet minister who organises the Government's business in the Commons, working closely with the Government Chief Whip, and makes the business statement every sitting Thursday.
roles.youth: After Thursday's statement MPs question the Leader, often asking for a debate on an issue: a route your MP can use for yours.

roles.d: MPs and peers appointed by their party to make sure colleagues vote with the party, organise business, pass on information, and allocate their party's places on select committees. Party discipline is looser in the Lords.
roles.youth: Whips decide a lot about which Bills move and when; MPs' votes often follow the whip.

roles.role: Leader of the House of Lords
roles.d: The Government's leader in the Lords. Because the Lord Speaker cannot rule on procedure, the Leader advises the House on procedure and order.
roles.youth: In the Lords, peers largely police their own debates: there is no Speaker calling people to order.

roles.d: Presides over business in the Lords Chamber from the Woolsack, chairs the House of Lords Commission and acts as an ambassador for the House. Unlike the Commons Speaker, the Lord Speaker has no power to rule on procedure; the House governs itself, advised by the Leader.
roles.youth: A useful contrast with the Commons Speaker for a citizenship lesson.

roles.d: Crossbench peers are independents with no whip. They elect a Convenor from among themselves to keep them informed and speak for the group on key occasions; the Convenor sits on the House's main domestic committees.
roles.youth: Crossbenchers can swing close votes, so their views matter to any campaign at Lords stage.

roles.d: A select committee of MPs that considers how the Commons conducts its public business and recommends changes to its rules. The Lords has its own Procedure Committee, appointed each session.
roles.youth: If a rule of debate seems unfair, this is the committee that can recommend changing it.

roles.d: Non-party officials who advise members on procedure. In the Commons, members can ask the Table Office about anything in the Order Paper.
roles.youth: Clerks also support the Youth Select Committee, so young people work with them directly.

building.what: Fire destroys most of the medieval Palace of Westminster. Westminster Hall survives.
A public competition for a new Palace. Entries had to be Gothic or Elizabethan and anonymous; 97 were submitted. Charles Barry won, working with Augustus Welby Pugin, then 23.
Each anonymous entry carried a small symbol. Barry chose the portcullis from the Henry VII chapel next door. It is now the symbol of UK Parliament.
Pugin designed most of the Palace's ornate interiors, carvings and furniture. The Palace is counted among the finest Gothic Revival buildings in the world.
The rebuilt Palace opens; the State Opening ceremony used today dates from then.
Both Houses set up the Restoration and Renewal Programme, Parliament agrees in 2018 that the work must be done, and a 2019 Act sets out how it will be delivered.
The Restoration and Renewal Client Board publishes costed proposals for the work.
The National Audit Office reports on the Programme as Parliament is asked to narrow four options to two, warning that inaction is itself a choice with serious consequences.

building_note: Further reading: historian and former parliamentary archivist Dr Caroline Shenton's books tell the story of the fire and the rebuild.
rules_intro: Parliament's rules (Standing Orders in the Commons) are not fixed. Committees of members review them and recommend changes, and the House decides.

rules.d: The Procedure Committee, set up under Standing Order 147, considers the practice and procedure of the House in the conduct of public business and makes recommendations.
The House of Lords has its own Procedure Committee with a similar job, appointed in each session.
In 2026 the Lords consulted on sitting earlier on Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Its committee expects to report in January 2027, and the House will then decide.
The Procedure Committee's inquiries and reports are listed on its own pages; in 2026 it took evidence on written parliamentary questions.

rules.t: Why a youth campaigner should care
rules.d: How long a debate lasts, who gets called and how questions are answered all shape whether an issue is heard. Rules that seem unfair can be changed, through the members who sit on these committees.
